summary: Describes the objects needed to hold information about IP networks and IP numbers in the X.500 Directory. It builds on the framework in RFC 1609 for representing networks in the Directory. It is experimental.

eli5.summary: A big phone book can also list the networks themselves. This explains how to write down network information in that phone book.

questions: how to store ip networks in x.500
subtitle: A schema for storing IP networks and addresses in a directory service.

tldr.problem: IP network information is currently managed centrally by a few authorities. As the Internet grows, this centralized approach becomes a bottleneck. There is no standardized way to represent IP networks, routing policies, and autonomous systems in a distributed directory.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1608 extends the X.500 Directory framework with object classes for IP networks, nodes, interfaces, and autonomous systems. It defines how to store delegation hierarchies, routing policies, and mappings from IP addresses to network elements.
tldr.outcome: Organizations can now represent their IP infrastructure in X.500, enabling distributed management of IP assignments and network information. The RFC is Experimental.

today: RFC 1608 is Experimental. While the X.500 Directory model was theoretically sound, the X.500 technology itself never gained widespread adoption in the Internet. Most IP address management today uses WHOIS and later RDAP (Registry Data Access Protocol) for querying IP registries rather than X.500.

sections.title: Centralized Management Is a Bottleneck
sections.content: The RFC opens with a clear problem. In 1994, a handful of organizations—IANA, network registries, NICs, and the NSFNET NOC—maintain all IP network infrastructure information centrally. This worked when the Internet was small, but as growth exploded, the centralized approach became a bottleneck. Each change had to go through the same channels. The RFC proposes using the X.500 Directory, a distributed system where information is mastered locally by the organization responsible for it, but globally queryable.
sections.eli5: In 1994, only a few people kept track of all the world's computer networks. As the Internet grew, this became too slow. The RFC proposes a way for each organization to keep track of its own networks.

sections.title: Images and Objects in the Directory
sections.content: The RFC defines two categories of directory objects. IP images—called ipNetworkImage, ipNodeImage, and ipNetworkInterfaceImage—are views of network elements, describing the technical and administrative properties of networks and hosts. These live under the organization that runs them. IP namespace objects—delegatedBlock, ipGroup, and ipReference—form a separate, hierarchical tree tracking which IP addresses have been assigned to whom and when. This split allows an organization to describe both the physical infrastructure and the administrative assignment hierarchy.
sections.eli5: The directory can store two kinds of information: what a network looks like (its speed, location, who manages it) and who owns which IP addresses (who got them assigned when).

sections.title: The IP Address Hierarchy
sections.content: IP addresses are delegated in a hierarchical structure. A top-level authority assigns a block of addresses to a regional NIC. That NIC can delegate sub-blocks to local authorities, creating a tree. The RFC models this with delegatedBlock objects, where each block has a lower and upper bound. Under each delegatedBlock, ipGroup objects represent individual network numbers. An ipGroup points to an ipNetworkImage describing that network. Finally, ipReference objects represent single host addresses, each pointing to an ipNodeImage. This structure mirrors the actual allocation hierarchy and makes it possible to identify the administrator of any address by following the tree upward.
sections.eli5: IP addresses are like postal codes. A big organization gets a range of codes. They can subdivide it and give pieces to smaller organizations. The directory shows this tree of who owns which numbers.

sections.title: Network Images and Routing Policy
sections.content: An ipNetworkImage stores technical details: the network number, network mask (supporting classless networking), associated domain names, the inaddr server, the provider, and the online date. For routing, an asNumber field links the network to its Autonomous System. Autonomous System objects (asObject) store routing policies—the asIn, asOut, and asDefault attributes encode rules about which routes the AS accepts and announces. While not fast enough for real-time routing, this representation serves network management and planning. For instance, a network management tool could query the directory to find alternate paths that respect published routing policies.
sections.eli5: Each network can say which other networks it is willing to send traffic to and from. This doesn't happen in real time, but it helps people understand the rules.

sections.title: Living with Duplication and Future Integration
sections.content: The RFC acknowledges a practical problem: most organizations do not yet have entries in the X.500 Directory. So NICs will keep copies of necessary organizational information locally, in an "affiliated organizations" subtree, to avoid breaking existing workflows. When organizations set up their own X.500 directories, the RFC recommends using X.525 shadowing mechanisms to keep the information synchronized, delegating the consistency burden to the Directory itself. This pragmatic approach allows deployment to start even before the full Directory infrastructure is in place.
sections.eli5: Not everyone has a phone book entry yet. So the network information centers will keep local copies for now. Later, when everyone has a phone book, they can share the real copies and keep them in sync automatically.

sections.title: No Security Discussion
sections.content: The RFC section on security is minimal, acknowledging that security issues are not discussed in the memo. This is typical of infrastructure-layer protocols from that era, where the focus was on the mechanism rather than threat models.
sections.eli5: The RFC does not talk about security. It assumes the directory itself handles access control and that operators will decide who can see what.
